parole.testo: Borrowed from Parthian 𐫀𐫁𐫅𐫏𐫗 (ʾbdyn /⁠aβδēn⁠/, “custom, habit; customary, usual; manner, way”), from Proto-Iranian *HabidáyHanaH. Related to օրինակ (ōrinak). Dubblete آیین (āyēn)
From Proto-Iranian *ā-rām(a)-, from *ā- (“ad-”) + *rām- (“calm”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“at”) + *h₁rem- (“to rest”).

From Proto-Iranian *ā- + *saima- (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skeh₂i-), perhaps borrowed from a prefixed form of Sogdian 𐼼𐼷𐼺 (sym /⁠sēm⁠/, “confused, trouble”) with final denasalization; cf. Classical Persian آسیمه (āsēma, “confused”). Compare Ancient Greek σκαιός (skaiós, “left-hand, clums

Émile Benveniste claims that āl-γonak, the precursor of modern آلگونه (âlgune), is attested and connects this to the Persian female name Ἀλογούνη (Alogoúnē) mentioned in Ctesias. Harold Walter Bailey suggests that this is a merger of two Proto-Iranian [Term?] roots, *āla- and *harda-, cf. Avestan 𐬵𐬀

Of uncertain origin. Cheung derives the verb from Proto-Iranian *ā- (“ad-”) + *dauH- (“to smear, rub (on)”), with a lambdacism of *d > l. The prefix is from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“to, at”), while the verbal root is of uncertain further origin, with possible connections to Vedic Sanskrit आधावति

From Proto-Iranian *āmaH-, from Proto-Iranian *ā- + *maH- (“to measure”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *maH-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“at”) + *meh₁- (“to measure”). Compare آماده (âmâde, “ready”), Avestan 𐬁𐬨𐬁𐬙𐬀- (āmāta-), Sanskrit माति (māti, “measure, knowledge”), Ancient Greek μῆτῐς (mêtĭs, “sk

From Proto-Iranian *ā- + *gam- (“to come”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“to, at”) + *gʷem- (“to walk, to step, to come”); exact cognate with English advent, and partial cognate with English come. The present stem comes from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ey- (“to go”).
From Proto-Iranian *Hanguǰatu.
Ultimately from Proto-Iranian [Term?], compare Khotanese [script needed] (tsāṣṭa-, “calm”).
From Proto-Iranian *wayǰ-, from Proto-Indo-European *weyg-.
From Proto-Iranian *ā- (“ad-”) + *kánHati (“to dig”). The prefix is from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“to, at”).

From Proto-Iranian *abi-ra(n)ǰ- (“to color, dye”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)reg-. Cognate with Ancient Greek ῥέζω (rhézō, “I dye, paint”) and Persian رنگ (rang) itself; also an exact doublet of اورنگ (owrang) / افرنگ (afrang, “throne; splendor”). Compare Old Armenian ապարանջան (aparanǰan) and Ge

Attested late; first attestation may be Mullā Tughrā (died 1667). From a suffixed form of Proto-Iranian *ák- (“bad”), related to Proto-Indo-European *ákas (“bad”). Compare Avestan 𐬀𐬑𐬙𐬌 (axti, “pain, suffering”) and Sanskrit अक (aka, “pain”).
From Proto-Iranian *Hárǰati, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hárǰʰati, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elgʷʰ-.
Inherited from Proto-Iranian *spr̥jā́.

A saponin-containing “washing-herb”, a derivative of the root Proto-Iranian *snaH- (“to wash, swim”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂- (“to swim”). Borrowed from Middle Iranian also into Old Armenian աւշնան (awšnan) and Arabic أُشْنَان (ʔušnān). The preverb participating in the derivation is dispu

A suffixed form of Proto-Iranian *Hácru, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éḱru (“tear”). It may have been borrowed from Parthian 𐫀𐫢𐫐 (ʾšk /⁠ašk⁠/) or some other Iranian language. Doublet of ارس (ars), which was inherited and lacks the suffix. Compare Khotanese [script needed] (āṣka-), Wakhi yašk.
From Proto-Iranian [Term?], from Proto-Indo-Iranian [Term?]. Cognate with Sanskrit अणक (aṇaka, “contemptible, insignificant”).
From Proto-Iranian *Hángištah, from Proto-Iranian *Hángārah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hángāras, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óngʷl̥ (“charcoal”).

From Middle Persian [script needed] (SLYA) / [script needed] (wt' /⁠wad⁠/, “bad, evil”), from Proto-Iranian *watah, with further origin uncertain. Akin to Old Armenian վատ (vat), an Iranian borrowing. Unrelated to English bad, despite phonetic and semantic similarity.

parole.significato: to bear; to carry; to take
parole.testo: From Middle Persian [Book Pahlavi needed] (bwltn' /⁠burtan⁠/, “carry, take”), from Old Persian 𐎲𐎼𐎫𐎡𐎹 (b-r-t-i-y /⁠baratiy⁠⁠/), from Proto-Iranian *bárati, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *bʰárati, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti. Cognate to Pashto وړل (wṛəl), Kurdish birin, English bear, and Russian брать

Ultimately from Proto-Iranian *varn-aka-, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *wr̥Hánas, from Proto-Indo-European *urh₁en- (“ram”). See also Mazanderani وره (vare), Sanskrit उरण (úraṇa), Central Kurdish بەرخ (berx), Northern Kurdish berx, Zazaki verek, Baluchi گْوّرگ (gwarag), Ancient Greek ἀρήν (arḗn), Old Arm
From Proto-Iranian *band-, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *bʰandʰ-, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to bind”); cognate to English bend, bind.

parole.significato: band, tie, fastening, ligature, bandage, chain, shackle, fetter
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Persian *bandah, from Proto-Iranian *bandáh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *bʰandʰás, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to bind”). Compare Old Armenian բանտ (bant, “prison”), an Iranian borrowing. More at band, bind. Doublet of باند (bând).

From Middle Persian [Term?] ŠPYL / wyh (weh, “better, good”), from Old Persian *vahuš (“good”), from Proto-Iranian *Hwáhuš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hwásuš, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wésus (“good”). Northern Luri بێ (bı). Related to Old Armenian վեհ (veh, “sublime”), an Iranian borrowin
From Proto-Iranian *wábžah (“wasp”).

Inherited from Proto-Iranian [Term?]; compare Pashto بيزو (bízo, “monkey”). Anciently borrowed into Old East Slavic обезьꙗ́на (obezĭjána) whence Russian обезья́на (obezʹjána, “monkey, ape”), and likely into Old Turkic 𐰋𐰃𐰲𐰃𐰤 (béčin, “monkey”).
Inherited from Middle Persian [script needed] (wck' /⁠waččag⁠/, “child, baby, cub”), from Proto-Iranian *wacáh (“calf”).
Ultimately inherited from Proto-Iranian *waixa (“base, root”).

parole.significato: a camel's colt two years old
parole.testo: From Proto-Iranian *bi-sāradiyakah (compare *carHdáh (“year”)).
Inherited from Proto-Iranian *tāp-, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *tāpás, from Proto-Indo-European *tep-.
Inherited from Proto-Iranian *tāp-, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *temp-, extended form of *ten- (“to stretch”).
From Proto-Iranian *tāp- (“to twist, wind”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *temp- (“to span, stretch, extend”).
Inherited from Proto-Iranian *tatr̥wáh.
Ultimately inherited from Proto-Iranian *tr̥fšah.
Cognate with Parthian 𐫤𐫜𐫡 (tfr /⁠tafr⁠/, “cheese”), from Proto-Iranian *tr̥práh.

From Proto-Iranian, from Proto-Indo-Iranian, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ptyēw- (“to spit, vomit”). Akin to Ossetian ту (tu, “spittle”), Sanskrit ष्ठीवति (ṣṭhīvati, “to spit”), Armenian թուք (tʻukʻ, “spit, spittle”), Serbo-Croatian pljuvati (“to spit”), Ancient Greek πτύω (ptúō, “to spit out”), Lat
From Proto-Iranian *tafšcáti, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *tapsćáti, from Proto-Indo-European *tep- (“to be warm, tepid”).

From Proto-Iranian *tánHtā, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *tánHtar-, from Proto-Indo-European *ténh₂-tōr or *tónh₂-tōr, whence Latin tonitrus may also be derived; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder, resound”). Compare similarly *tónh₂-r̥, whence Germanic and Celtic cognates. Cogna

From Proto-Iranian *taw(H)táH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *taw(H)táH (“people, folk, crowd”), from Proto-Indo-European *tew(H)téh₂ (“people, tribe, men-at-arms”). Cognate with Northern Kurdish tûde, Sogdian 𐫤𐫇𐫔𐫏𐫍 (twδyh /⁠tūδē⁠/). More distantly related to Latin tōtus, Latvian tàuta, Lithuanian tautà,

parole.significato: to search; to seek; to look for
parole.testo: From Proto-Iranian *Hyawd- (“to fight, struggle (for something), strive, seek”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hyawdʰ- (“to fight, struggle”).

جوجه (juje) + تیغی (tiġi), literally “spiky chicken”, as per folk etymology. But جوجه (juje) probably does not mean chicken or chick here, but is instead altered pronunciation of Classical Persian ژوژه (žuža, “hedgehog”), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *ǰúǰakah (“hedgehog”).
From Proto-Iranian *haxšuka, from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”). Cognate with Proto-Germanic *sahsą (“knife”).
Inherited from Proto-Iranian *Hhučiθráh (composed of *Hhu- (“good”) and *čiθráh (“appearance, likeness; face”)), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hsučitrás.
From خدا (xudaā /xodaâ, “God”) + داد (dād /dâd, past stem of دادن (dādan /dâdan, “to give”)). See Proto-Iranian *BágadaHtah.
From Proto-Iranian *xrā́š- (“to scratch”), probably of sound-symbolic origin, similar to English scratch and German kratzen (“to scratch”).
Inherited from Proto-Iranian *Hhúškah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hsúškas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂sews- + *-kos. Cognate with Sanskrit शुष्क (śuṣka).
From Proto-Iranian *axšáyHnah (“blue; green”). Compare Ossetian ӕхсин (æxsin).
Related to the verb خفیدن (xafidan, “to choke; to cough”), from Proto-Iranian *xaf- (“to cough”), ultimately onomatopoeic.

Presumably related to چمیدن (čamidan, “to twist, bend”), چفته (čaftah, “curved, bent; vaulted roof”), from Proto-Iranian *čámpati ~ *kapánti (“to bend”), ultimately of unknown origin. Cognate with Parthian 𐫗𐫐𐫖𐫁𐫏𐫅 (nkmbyd /⁠rikambēd⁠/, “to bend”).
Akin to Old Armenian խոհ (xoh), an Iranian borrowing.
From Proto-Iranian *hwarda-. Cognate with Northern Kurdish xwelî, which see for more.

Inherited from Proto-Iranian *hwanH- (“to call”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *swanH-, from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound”). Compare Northern Kurdish xwendin, Northern Luri هںنێ (hənı), Latin sonō, Sanskrit स्वनति (svanati).

From Middle Persian 𐭧𐭥𐭡 (xūb), from Old Persian *huvāpah, from Proto-Iranian *HhuHā́pah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *HsuHápas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁su- (“good”) + *h₃épos (“work”). Compare Sogdian [script needed] (xwp).
Inherited from Proto-Iranian *húHar, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *súHar, from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥.

Inherited from Middle Persian 𐭣𐭬𐭩𐭠 (DMYA /⁠xōn⁠/), also 𐫑𐫇𐫗 (k̇wn /⁠xōn⁠/), from Proto-Iranian *wahūnī. Cognate with Bakhtiari خین (xīn), Northern Luri خی (xi), Baluchi ہون (hōn), Northern Kurdish xwîn, Central Kurdish خوێن (xwên), Southern Kurdish خۊن (xün) or خوین (xuyn), Zazaki goni, Gurani ۋنی (
From Proto-Iranian. Compare Khotanese [script needed] (khīra, “depressed; sad”), Khwarezmian [Term?] (/⁠xyrʾw⁠/), Sogdian [Term?] (/⁠xyrʾk⁠/, “stupid”).

From Proto-Iranian *haič- (“to pour”), from Proto-Indo-European *seykʷ- (“to moisten”). Cognate with Sanskrit सेक (seka, “sprinkling; moistening”), Ancient Greek ἰκμᾰ́ς (ikmắs, “wetness”), possibly Proto-Germanic *saiwiz (“sea, lake, ocean”).

Inherited from Middle Persian [script needed] (dʾlwkˈ /⁠dārūg⁠/, “drug, medicament”), perhaps from Proto-Iranian *dā́rukah (“tree, wood”). Compare Parthian 𐫅𐫀𐫓𐫇𐫃 (dʾlwg /⁠dālūg⁠/, “plant, tree”). Unrelated to English drug.

From Middle Persian [Book Pahlavi needed] (dlht'), [Book Pahlavi needed] (dlʾht'), 𐫅𐫡𐫟𐫤 (drxt /⁠draxt⁠/, “tree”), from Proto-Iranian *draxta- (“firmly standing”), with the first part deriving from Proto-Iranian *drag- (“to hold, strengthen”), itself related to Proto-Iranian *dā́ru (“wood, tree”) and

From Proto-Iranian *dr̥ti- (“manure, feces”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰṛ-to-, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreyd- (“to have diarrhea”), whence also English dirt, Old Norse dríta (“to defecate”), and Russian дриста́ть (dristátʹ, “to shart”). Possibly related to Proto-Indo-European *dʰerh₃- (“to spri
Inherited from Proto-Iranian *drauH-. Cognate with Pashto لو (law, “reaping, harvest”).
Inherited from Proto-Iranian *dā́ru, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *dā́ru, from Proto-Indo-European *dóru. Also see دار (dār /dâr), درخت (daraxt). Aghwan 𐔳𐕒𐕡𐕙𐕒𐕡𐔳 (durud) is an Iranian borrowing.
From or related to Proto-Iranian *duš-. Cognate with Sanskrit दुष्ट (duṣṭa).

From Middle Persian [script needed] (dwšmn'), [script needed] (dwšmyn'), 𐫅𐫇𐫢𐫖𐫏𐫗 (dwšmyn /⁠dušmēn⁠/, “enemy”), from Proto-Iranian *dušmánāh. Compare Ancient Greek δῠσμενής (dŭsmenḗs), Sanskrit दुर्मनस् (durmanas).

From Middle Persian 𐭣𐭩𐭫 (dyl /⁠dil⁠/), from Proto-Iranian *jā́rd, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ȷ́ʰā́rd, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr; with a regular phonetic shift *ȷ́ŕ̥d- > *dŕ̥d > *dŕ̥l > dil. For the phonetic change, compare گل (gol) and سالار (sâlâr). Cognates with Parthian 𐫉𐫏𐫡𐫅 (zyrd /⁠
From Proto-Iranian *danHáyati, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *dʰanHáyati, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰenh₂-. Cognate with Sanskrit धन् (dhan, “to cause to move”).
From Proto-Iranian *duHmáh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *dʰuHmás, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós. Compare Northern Kurdish dû and Lurish دی (di, “smoke”).

Inherited from Proto-Iranian *duHráh (“far”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *duHrás (“far”), from Proto-Indo-European *dweh₂rós, from *dweh₂- + *-rós. Cognate with Central Kurdish دوور (dûr, “far, distant”), Northern Luri دیر (dir), Pashto لرې (lëre, “distant”), Sanskrit दूर (dūra, “distant, remote”), Ave
From Proto-Iranian *Har- (“to set in motion”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er- (“to move, set in motion”). Cognate with English run.
From Proto-Iranian *Hragúš. Conflated partially with Arabic راووق (“strainer”).

Inherited from Proto-Iranian *rax-ta- (literally “colored”), ultimately from the same root as رنگ (rang). Cognate with Sanskrit रक्त (raktá, “red; coloured, dyed”), Khotanese رختک (rxtk /⁠raxtak⁠/, “red”).
Inherited from Proto-Iranian, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-. Akin to Old Armenian երախտիք (eraxtikʻ), an Iranian borrowing.

parole.significato: coloured red and white; spotted red or white.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Iranian *ra(n)ǰ- (“to colour, dye”) (compare Sogdian [script needed] (rɣš- /⁠raxš⁠/, “Rakhsh”), Khwarezmian رختک (rxtk /⁠raxtak⁠/, “red”), Mazanderani رش (raš, “reddish-brown”), Northern Kurdish reş (“black”), Talysh رش (rəş, “light brown”)), from Proto-Indo-Iranian (compare Sa
From Proto-Iranian *rúxš (“to shine”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-. Cognate with Ossetian рухс (ruxs, “light”).
From Proto-Iranian *rauxšn- (“to shine”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright, to shine, to see”).

From Proto-Iranian *raz- (“to leave, escape (one's notice)”), related to Proto-Indo-Iranian *raȷ́ʰ- (“to abandon”). Cognate with Sanskrit रहति (rahati, “to abandon”) and रहस्य (rahasya, “mystery”); see the latter for more.
From Proto-Iranian *Hráwdah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hráwdʰas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“to grow”). Indo-Iranian cognates include Baluchi ردگ (ruddag) and Sanskrit रोधति (rodhati).

From Proto-Iranian *wrais- (“to turn, to spin”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian, from Proto-Indo-European *wriḱ-yé-ti (“to twist, to bend”), whence also Avestan 𐬎𐬭𐬎𐬎𐬌𐬯𐬌𐬀 (uruuisia, “to turn”), German reihen (“to sew loosely”), English wry, Latin rīca (“veil”). Doublet of رشته (rešte, “thread, string”).

From Proto-Iranian *ra(n)ǰ- (“to colour, dye”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian [Term?]. Cognate with Sanskrit रञ्ज् (rañj, “to be dyed or coloured, to redden, grow red, glow”). Related to رنگ (rang, “color”).
From Proto-Iranian *Hrum-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rew-. Cognate with English ruin.
From Proto-Iranian *Hrawtáh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hrawtás.
Earlier attested as راوچه, ultimately from Proto-Iranian *Hragúš.
Ultimately from Proto-Iranian *jāráyati. See it for more.
From Proto-Iranian *jyáh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ȷ́ʰyás.

Probably ultimately a derivative of Proto-Iranian *zanH- (“to give birth; to be born”) and thus related to Sogdian [script needed] (zʾk /⁠zāk⁠/, “child”), Middle Persian [Book Pahlavi needed] (zhk'), 𐫉𐫍𐫃 (zhg /⁠zahag⁠/, “offspring, child”), Parthian 𐫉𐫍𐫃 (zhg /⁠zahag⁠/, “offspring, child”), Persian ز

From Proto-Iranian *jā́nu, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ȷ́ā́nu, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu. Cognate with Mazanderani زندی (zendi), Ancient Greek γόνυ (gónu), Latin genū, English knee. Doublet of گونیا.
From Proto-Iranian [Term?], from Proto-Indo-Iranian [Term?], from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰer-, *gʰer- (“to encircle; to spin around”).
From Proto-Iranian [Term?], from Proto-Indo-Iranian [Term?], from Proto-Indo-European *ǵerh₂- (“to grow old, to mature”).
From Proto-Iranian *jaluš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ȷ́aluš, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵelu-. Akin to Old Armenian տզրուկ (tzruk), an Iranian borrowing.
Ultimately from Proto-Iranian *jar-, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ȷ́ar-, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵwelH- (“to burn, shine”). Compare Proto-Germanic *kulą (“coal”), Irish gual (“coal”).

Or زیفتن. Ultimately a derivation of Proto-Iranian *zay- (“to equip, to adorn”), with no apparent cognates outside of Iranian. Related to زیور (zivar, “ornament”). Compare Baluchi [script needed] (ázit, “to embellish, adorn”).

From Proto-Iranian *ǰáyHati, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ǰáyHati, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷéyh₃eti (“to live”), from the root *gʷeyh₃-. Cognate with Avestan 𐬘𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (juuaⁱti), Northern Kurdish jîyan, Pashto ژوند کول (žwënd kawël), Sanskrit जीवति (jīvati). More distantly related to Ancient Greek βείο
From Middle Persian s’htn' (sāxtan, “to build, make”), from Proto-Iranian *cāčáyati (“to prepare, build”). Cognate with Sanskrit शक् (śak, “to be able, capable”); see there for more cognates.
Ultimately from Proto-Iranian *cánhati; see there for more. Cognate with Sanskrit शंसति (śáṃsati, “to declare”), Latin cēnseō and perhaps Ancient Greek κῶμος (kômos).

Inherited from Proto-Iranian [Term?], cognate to Ossetian синдзӕ (sinʒæ, “thorn”) and Khotanese śīṃja (“thorny jujube”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“thorn-like”), related to اسپناج (espanâj, “spinach”).

From Proto-Iranian *snušáH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *snušáH, from Proto-Indo-European *snusós (“daughter-in-law”). Cognate with Sanskrit स्नुषा (snuṣā́, “daughter-in-law”), Latin nurus, Ancient Greek νυός (nuós), Old English snoru.

From Middle Persian [script needed] (sahm), from Old Persian [script needed] (*çahman), from Proto-Iranian *θráhma, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *trásma, from Proto-Indo-European *trés-mn̥, from *tres- (“to tremble”). Doublet of رم (ram, “shying”).

From Middle Persian [Book Pahlavi needed] (spwlyk' /⁠spurrīg⁠/, “entire, complete, perfect”), from Proto-Iranian *uc- + *pr̥Hnáh (“full, filled”). Compare Old Armenian սպառ (spaṙ, “completion”), an Iranian borrowing.

From Proto-Iranian *skarf- (“to stumble”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷʰh₂el- (“to stumble”). Cognate with Sanskrit स्खल् (skhal, “to stumble, fail”), Ancient Greek σφάλλω (sphállō, “to bring down”), σφάλλομαι (sphállomai, “to fall”), Old Armenian սխալեմ (sxalem, “to stumble, fail”), and possibly
From Proto-Iranian *sikurnah (compare Avestan 𐬯𐬎𐬐𐬎𐬭𐬆𐬥𐬀 (sukurəna), Sogdian [script needed] (syrrn /⁠sērn⁠/), Pashto شکوڼ (škuṇ)).
Ultimately derived from Proto-Iranian *cráwniš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćráwniš, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlównis.

Inherited from Proto-Iranian *gžárati, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *gžʰárati, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰgʷʰéreti (“to flow, to melt”). Cognate with Avestan 𐬖𐬲𐬀𐬭𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (γžaraⁱti), Ancient Greek φθείρω (phtheírō) and Sanskrit क्षरति (kṣarati, “to flow, stream, trickle”).
Inherited from Proto-Iranian *xšáfnyah, from *xšápā or *-yah.
Inherited from Proto-Iranian *xšaita-varta.
